title: Guan Yu's Bone Scraping: Hua Tuo Couldn't Make It? The Novel Is Off by at Least 11 Years
description:
Guan Yu plays a board game while Hua Tuo scrapes his bone: you've surely seen it. We compare the books that told it. The Biography of Guan Yu in Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms takes just 85 characters: "Yu was once hit by a stray arrow that pierced his left arm"; it healed but ached on rainy days; a doctor said "poisoned arrowhead, poison in the bone"; he had it cut open while, by chance, dining with his generals, "talking and laughing as ever." Left arm; no board, no Ma Liang, no doctor's name, no year. Only the next passage dates Fancheng: Jian'an 24 (219), when Pang De "shot Yu in the forehead". The historical Hua Tuo was Cao Cao's doctor; he pleaded a sick wife, was jailed at Xu and "tortured to death". When his beloved son Cangshu (Cao Chong) lay dying, Cao Cao said: "I regret killing Hua Tuo; the boy dies needlessly." Cao Chong died in Jian'an 13 (208), so Hua Tuo was dead by 208 at the latest, and the Romance of the Three Kingdoms' Hua Tuo scene at Fancheng is at least 11 years too late. Neither biography mentions the other, so we can't say the doctor of the history's undated surgery was surely not Hua Tuo. A Northern Zhou stele says "more bone scraping and medicine than Guan Yu" and an early Yuan historian copied the passage; neither names the doctor. The earliest book we've found naming him is the Sanguozhi Pinghua (Yuan, Zhizhi era): Hua Tuo, "a man in the traitor Cao's hands", goes to Jingzhou. The Ming Romance moves it to Fancheng, makes it the right arm and adds Ma Liang's game; its standard edition even has Hua Tuo die in Cao Cao's jail for mentioning the scraping.

Texts: histories, a fixed-edition digital transcription, Daizhige, Wikisource; Pinghua, Daizhige; Jiajing edition, Wikisource (no scan check); standard edition, Project Gutenberg. Jin and Yuan plays not checked; no medical explanations. Sources: references below.

AI-generated illustrations; historical figures are unnamed cartoons, not likenesses.

kg101.text: You've seen it: Guan Yu plays a board game as Hua Tuo scrapes his bone. No wince.

kg102.text: But the official history has just 85 characters; several things you picture aren't in it.

kg103.text: The novel: a poison arrow hits Guan Yu's right arm at Fancheng.

kg104.text: A boat comes from Jiangdong; the doctor ashore says his surname is Hua, his name Tuo.

kg105.text: Oddly, in the official history, Hua Tuo was Cao Cao's doctor;

kg106.text: and Guan Yu is now attacking Cao Cao's city of Fancheng.

kg107.text: And that's not the oddest: one regretful line from Cao Cao holds Hua Tuo, and a child.

kg108.text: A storyteller's text predating the novel invented Hua Tuo's past.

kg109.text: This file checks the books telling this surgery, from 3rd-century history to a Ming novel.

kg110.text: Did Hua Tuo really scrape Guan Yu's bone?

kg201.text: The novel says yes: Guan Ping at once asks, are you the one who treated Zhou Tai's wounds?

kg202.text: He nods. The novel really did show it earlier: Hua Tuo healed Zhou Tai in a month.

kg203.text: Guan Ping leads him in: Guan Yu is at a game with Ma Liang.

kg204.text: Guan Yu holds out his right arm. Hua Tuo's verdict?

kg205.text: Hua Tuo: it's an aconite-tipped crossbow bolt, and the poison is in the bone; untreated, the arm may be useless.

kg206.text: His plan: set up a post with an iron ring, tie the arm through it,

kg207.text: cover the head with a quilt, then cut.

kg208.text: Guan Yu laughs: so easy! Who needs a post and ring?

kg209.text: He calls for wine, has a few cups, plays on, and simply gives Hua Tuo his arm.

kg210.text: The novel says all who watch, inside and out, hide their faces and go pale. And Guan Yu?

kg211.text: He eats and drinks as if nothing's wrong.

kg212.text: Honestly, whenever I read this, I pity Ma Liang across the board.

kg213.text: When it's done, Guan Yu flexes his right arm: you're a divine healer, sir.

kg214.text: Hua Tuo, too: in a life of medicine, I've never seen such a patient.

kg215.text: He also warns: 100 days to heal, and no anger until then.

kg216.text: Guan Yu offers 100 taels of gold. Does Hua Tuo accept?

kg217.text: No. He leaves a remedy and goes.

kg218.text: Almost every detail you picture is in this one chapter.

kg219.text: But how much of it is left in Chen Shou's history?

kg301.text: The answer is in those 85 characters from the start: Chen Shou's Biography of Guan Yu.

kg302.text: It opens: "A stray arrow once hit Yu, piercing his left arm."

kg303.text: Stray means no one knows who shot it; nor does Chen Shou name the battle.

kg304.text: The left arm. In the novel at the start, it was the right; here it's the other arm.

kg305.text: Stranger still, it's not a fresh wound: it had long healed, but the bone ached whenever it rained.

kg306.text: You probably know someone whose knees ache when it rains; for Guan Yu, it was that arm.

kg307.text: A doctor said: "Poisoned arrowhead; poison in the bone."

kg308.text: Open the arm, scrape the poison off the bone; only then is it cured for good.

kg309.text: In his place, you'd probably hesitate. And Guan Yu?

kg310.text: Without a word, Guan Yu held out his arm to be cut open.

kg311.text: The text has no post, no iron ring, no quilt over the head.

kg312.text: He happened to be hosting his generals; "shi" means by chance, not for show.

kg313.text: The text says he "carved the roast and drew the wine, talking and laughing as ever."

kg314.text: At the start I said several things you picture aren't there; here you see it: no board, no Ma Liang.

kg315.text: And the most important thing? The doctor's name?

kg316.text: None. The doctor shows up twice, both times just the word "yi", doctor.

kg317.text: Reading it first, I thought I'd skipped a line.

kg318.text: Pei Songzhi of the Southern Dynasties added many notes to the Records; here, none.

kg319.text: No name, but surely a year? Which year was this bone scraping?

kg401.text: The passage has no year at all, not even a season.

kg402.text: That "chang" in the first line means "once": Chen Shou inserts it, looking back.

kg403.text: Where? Right after Guan Yu writes to Zhuge Liang, asking how able Ma Chao, newly surrendered, is.

kg404.text: Ma Chao surrendered in the 19th year of Jian'an, 214 AD.

kg405.text: The question: does coming later mean it happened later?

kg406.text: Not necessarily. Placement shows where Chen Shou tells it, not what year it happened.

kg407.text: Only in the next passage does Chen Shou write "24th year."

kg408.text: The 24th year of Jian'an, 219 AD: Liu Bei becomes King of Hanzhong and makes Guan Yu General of the Front.

kg409.text: That same year Guan Yu attacked Fancheng, held by Cao Ren. The result?

kg410.text: In autumn heavy rain swelled the Han River, and all seven armies Cao Cao sent to help were flooded.

kg411.text: From the order alone, you'd put the surgery in this year; I admit I nearly did.

kg412.text: But the text never says that earlier rain was this one.

kg413.text: As it happens, in the Fancheng year Guan Yu really was hit by an arrow. Where?

kg414.text: Fighting him, Cao's Pang De hit his forehead.

kg415.text: Not the arm. Unrelated to the surgery.

kg416.text: Yet the novel moves both the doctor and the surgery into this Fancheng year. Was Hua Tuo still alive then?

kg501.text: The Biography of Hua Tuo gives no death year but ties it to another's illness.

kg502.text: Hua Tuo may bring mafeisan to mind: drink it, you go dead drunk and numb, then he cuts.

kg503.text: He's the history's top surgeon; later writers casting him in seems logical, but that's my guess.

kg504.text: At the start I said he was Cao Cao's doctor: Cao's headaches left him dizzy and muddled; one needle from Hua Tuo fixed it.

kg505.text: Later, gravely ill, Cao Cao wanted Hua Tuo for himself.

kg506.text: But Hua Tuo was homesick. Citing a letter, he went home awhile; there, he pleaded a sick wife and kept delaying.

kg507.text: Cao Cao had it checked. The result?

kg508.text: His orders: if she's really ill, give 40 hu of adzuki beans and extend the leave; if not, arrest him.

kg509.text: Today that'd be your boss checking up on a sick day; only, if it's real, you get a pile of red beans.

kg510.text: It turned out false. Hua Tuo was hauled off to prison in Xu.

kg511.text: Xun Yu pleaded for him: his skill is real, lives hang on it; spare him.

kg512.text: Cao Cao: "Why worry? Is the world short of such rats?"

kg513.text: The biography ends it in four characters: "sui kao jing Tuo", tortured to death.

kg514.text: Near death, Hua Tuo gave a jailer a scroll: "This can save lives." Did the jailer dare?

kg515.text: No, fearing the law. Hua Tuo let it go, got fire and burned it.

kg516.text: I find this part a pity every time.

kg517.text: After Hua Tuo died, Cao Cao's headaches went on.

kg518.text: Cao Cao stayed defiant: Hua Tuo could cure me but left the root to seem vital; spared, he'd still never cure me.

kg519.text: That's Cao Cao's claim, not the biography's verdict.

kg520.text: But some time later, the tough talk turned to regret. Over whom?

kg601.text: His beloved son, Cangshu. The regretful line I mentioned at the start was said right then:

kg602.text: "I regret killing Hua Tuo; the boy dies needlessly."

kg604.text: You know him: Cao Chong, the boy who put an elephant on a big boat and marked the waterline to weigh it.

kg605.text: The Biography of Cao Chong: Cao Chong, styled Cangshu.

kg606.text: At 13 he fell gravely ill, and Cao Cao prayed for his life himself.

kg607.text: The boy died anyway. Cao Cao grieved deeply and wept whenever he spoke of it.

kg608.text: That was the 13th year of Jian'an; in our calendar, 208 AD.

kg609.text: So when did Hua Tuo die?

kg610.text: The Biography of Hua Tuo has "after Tuo died", then Cangshu's illness: Hua Tuo died first, by that year at latest.

kg611.text: Now set the Fancheng year from earlier beside it: 219, 11 years after Cangshu died.

kg612.text: I asked: was Hua Tuo alive at Fancheng? By this timeline, the novel's Hua Tuo could never get there.

kg613.text: Honestly, at this point I wonder if the novelist ever noticed.

kg614.text: But the timeline rules out only the novel's scene. What about Chen Shou's undated surgery?

kg701.text: The timeline alone can't exclude it: an undated surgery slips past it.

kg702.text: The Biography of Hua Tuo lists many patients, no Guan Yu; Guan Yu's has no Hua Tuo.

kg703.text: So if someone says the history proves it wasn't Hua Tuo, that's going too far: it just doesn't say.

kg704.text: So who first wrote the name Hua Tuo into this story?

kg705.text: Not Chen Shou. A Northern Zhou stele praises a general for more bone scraping than Guan Yu.

kg706.text: By then, bone scraping meant Guan Yu; the doctor still had no name.

kg707.text: Early in the Yuan, a historian rewriting Three Kingdoms history copied this passage. A name this time?

kg709.text: The blank stayed empty for about a thousand years.

kg801.text: The name came from that storyteller's text: the Sanguozhi Pinghua, printed in the Yuan's Zhizhi era.

kg802.text: Of books found so far, it's the first to name him, writing Tuo with the "ear" radical.

kg803.text: The oddity from the start, why Cao Cao's doctor treats Guan Yu, the Pinghua explains:

kg804.text: Hua Tuo, Cao's man, found him cruel and fled to Guan Yu in Jingzhou.

kg805.text: Here too, Guan Yu's arm aches on cloudy days, as in Chen Shou;

kg806.text: Surprisingly, that stray arrow, shooter unknown, gets an archer here: Han Fu of Wu.

kg807.text: The storytellers even cast the archer; I truly laughed at that.

kg808.text: The novel's earlier post and iron ring are already in the Pinghua; Guan Yu roars with laughter: I'm a real man, why fear this?

kg809.text: It also sets it before the Single Sword Meeting, like Chen Shou: not Fancheng.

kg810.text: So who moved it to Fancheng?

kg901.text: The opening scene's source: the Ming Romance of the Three Kingdoms, whose oldest surviving edition has a 1522 preface.

kg902.text: Better yet, the novel moves Hua Tuo's death later too. To when?

kg903.text: After Guan Yu dies. Cao Cao has headaches; Hua Tuo offers to open his skull.

kg904.text: He cites Guan Yu: I scraped poison from his bone, and he showed no fear.

kg905.text: The standard edition has Cao Cao suspicious at once: you were close to Guan Yu; want revenge for him?

kg906.text: So Hua Tuo is thrown in prison and dies there.

kg907.text: In the novel, ironically, what dooms Hua Tuo is scraping Guan Yu's bone.

kg908.text: Back to the opening question: did Hua Tuo scrape Guan Yu's bone?

kg909.text: Remember the 11 years? By the historical timeline, the novel's Hua Tuo can't make it;

kg910.text: and Chen Shou's doctor still has no name today.

kg911.text: First image of Guan Yu's surgery: dinner table or game board? Tell me.

kg912.text: This channel sticks to what's in the records; subscribe to open files with me.
